ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: As shown in the figure, the uniform magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface, and the magnetic induction intensity is B. A group of ions of a certain charge-to-mass ratio q/m and speed magnitude v are emitted from the origin O with a certain divergence angle α, the y-axis exactly bisects this divergence angle, and after deflection the ion beam hits the x-axis within the region MN of length L. Find the expression for \(\cos(\alpha/2)\).

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, the uniform magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface, and the magnetic induction intensity is B. A group of ions of a certain charge-to-mass ratio q/m and speed magnitude v are emitted from the origin O with a certain divergence angle α, the y-axis exactly bisects this divergence angle, and after deflection the ion beam hits the x-axis within the region MN of length L. Find the expression for \(\cos(\alpha/2)\).
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the coordinate origin is O, the x-axis points to the right, and the y-axis points upward. The ion beam is emitted divergently upward from point O; in the figure, two oblique rays are used to represent the divergence boundaries, the included angle is marked as α, and the y-axis is located in the middle direction of this divergence angle. Two points M and N are marked on the positive direction of the x-axis, with N on the right side of M, indicating the interval MN on the x-axis where the ion beam hits after deflection, whose length is L. Reasoning: Let θ=α/2. Because the y-axis in the figure bisects the divergence angle, the central particle is emitted along the +y direction, and the two boundary particles respectively make an angle θ with the y-axis. The ions undergo uniform circular motion in the uniform magnetic field, and the Lorentz force provides the centripetal force, giving qvB=mv^2/R, so the trajectory radius is R=mv/(Bq). The initial velocity of the central particle is along the +y direction, its trajectory center is on the x-axis, and its trajectory intersects the x-axis again, apart from O, at the farthest point N, so ON=2R. The trajectory center of a boundary particle is determined by "the radius is perpendicular to the initial velocity"; the horizontal projection from its center to the y-axis is Rcosθ, so the other intersection point of this boundary circle with the x-axis is M, and OM=2Rcosθ. In the figure, the length of the hitting region MN is L, so L=ON-OM=2R-2Rcosθ=2R(1-cosθ). Thus cosθ=1-L/(2R). Substituting R=mv/(Bq), we obtain cos(α/2)=cosθ=1-BqL/(2mv).
